name: Jet
lede: Jet is a black gemstone made from fossilized wood, a hard, polishable lignite that Queen Victoria's long mourning turned into the color of grief and the livelihood of a Yorkshire fishing town.

sections.title: A word from Lycia
sections.body:
The English word comes from the Greek *gagates*, the name for a mineral from Gagas, the Roman name for Lycia, where it was mined; the English form is a corruption of *jayet* [1]. In ordinary speech *jet* has since become shorthand for a deep, glossy black: jet-black, or the rarer *jetty* [1]. Spanish keeps a different word, *azabache*, for the same stone [2].

The swatch needs a caveat. Our #343434 comes from the ISCC-NBS naming system of 1955, where jet is block 267, a very dark neutral grey with lightness 22 [9]. The stone itself is darker: our gem notes give about #131516 for polished jet and #343434 for rough [8].

sections.title: Wood that became a stone
sections.body:
Jet is not a mineral in the usual sense but was once alive [2]. It formed from forests that grew about 170 million years ago, made up of a single kind of conifer related to the monkey-puzzle tree, the genus *Araucaria* [2]. Logs buried in glutinous mud fossilized without air and shrank to a black layer an inch or so thick, which is why Whitby jet comes in thin seams under limestone [2]. St Clair calls it lignite, a hard coal that can be carved [3]. Pyrite, or fool's gold, sometimes grows alongside it and can make the surface sparkle [2].

Jet is soft by gem standards. The organic gemstones, which include jet, pearl and amber, are all softer than glass [6]. Rubbed, it picks up lint like [[gem:amber|amber]], and the English physician William Gilbert listed jet among the substances that behave this way when he named electricity in 1600 [7]. Finlay passes on a belief that warm jet could take fire by itself, and that Whitby shop owners sometimes arrived to find their stock burned, which she gives as local lore, not as a test result [2].

The reliable test is a scratch. Drawn across rough porcelain, real jet leaves a chocolate-brown streak, coal a black one, glass a white one and early vulcanite a grey one [2]. A hot needle also works: on real jet nothing happens, but plastic bubbles and smells sharp [2].

sections.title: The oldest black jewelry
sections.body:
People wore jet long before Victoria [2]. Skeleton 952 at the Roman fort of Catterick in north Yorkshire was buried with a necklace of more than 600 jet beads, about sixteen centuries ago [2]. Jet from Whitby turns up in Romano-British graves, and two finished rings and some rough jet from a Roman signal station at Kettleness suggest soldiers carved it on night watches [2]. A lathe-turned black flywheel from a spindle at the same site points to professional workers nearby [2].

Pliny says magicians once protected themselves with it, and Birren lists the medical claims attached to jet in old lore: it was said to heal epilepsy, toothache and glandular swellings [5]. These are beliefs recorded by a historian of amulets, not remedies, and none has support [5].

Spain kept the amulet tradition alive longest. Until the 1930s, children in Galicia wore black jet beads against the evil eye, and pilgrims arriving in Santiago de Compostela can still buy jet *figas*, carved hands with an extended finger, on Azabache Street [2].

sections.title: Whitby revived
sections.body:
Jet carving then lapsed in England [2]. Donne's poem 'A Jet Ring Sent' shows the stone had an ambiguous status in the seventeenth century, comparing a lover's fickle heart with the brittleness of a jet ring [2]. By Finlay's account England had no jet-workers around 1800, when a publican, John Carter, and his friend Robert Jefferson began whittling it in their spare time [2]. Once they employed a local turner, orders came from London [2]. By 1832 Whitby had two jet shops, and by 1850 seven men were calling themselves master jet-makers, one of them with 'Jet Ornament Maker to Her Majesty the Queen' above his door [2].

Part of the demand came from mourning shops on the Parisian model, which had supplied British women with the paraphernalia of grief since the 1840s [2].

sections.title: The color of mourning
sections.body:
Prince Albert died of typhoid fever on 14 December 1861, and within a week the crown jewelers were told to make black commemorative jewelry [3]. Queen Victoria stayed in mourning for the rest of her life, and she pressed black jewelry on her relatives for years [3]. Because glossy black jet could be worn at every stage of mourning, it sold in enormous numbers [3].

Books differ on the rule. Paterson's record of Victorian widows' mourning gives bombazine and heavy crepe for a year and a day, then black silk and jet jewelry for three months, then grey or mauve for the last six months [4]. St Clair says jet could be worn throughout mourning [3]. Both agree that the whole practice was strictly governed [3][4].

St Clair counts more than 1,400 men and boys employed by Whitby's jet industry in the 1870s, each earning three to four pounds a week [3]. The streets rang with the sound of trestle wheels making brooches, crucifixes and cameos, and some carvings were of fruit and flowers for the merely fashionable [2]. A New York department store advertised 'Whitby jet earrings' in its 1879–80 catalog [3].

sections.title: How a gem went out of fashion
sections.body:
The best Whitby jet was nearly used up by the 1880s; miners had been digging for it from the 1840s [3]. Carvers turned to softer, more brittle stone, a little from Poland and most from Spain, which chipped and lost its gloss [2][3]. Substitutes arrived: black cut glass called French jet, which Whitby men dismissed as 'bastard jet', black steel jewelry from Germany, and then vulcanite, an early plastic that was a decent visual and weight match [2][3]. Vulcanite makers learned to stain the surface brown so it would pass the streak test [2].

Fashion moved as well. By the 1880s the Queen herself wore pearls and diamonds, which Finlay calls white jewelry, and the public display of grief was starting to seem vulgar [2][3]. In 1926 Bertram Puckle wrote of the 'hideous lumps' of jet some still thought necessary in mourning [3]. By 1884 the industry supported only 300 jobs at about 25 shillings a week [3]. In 1936 only five jet workers remained [3].

Jet came back briefly in the 1990s and 2000s [2]. Whitby now draws thousands of visitors in dark clothes every May and October for its Dracula-themed weekends, and those who can afford it wear jet [2].

sections.title: The red devils
sections.body: Whitby jet-workers had a nickname, 'red devils', which Finlay says puzzled the people who revived the trade [2]. The London jeweler Hal Redvers-Jones, setting up shop at the foot of the abbey steps, found an old workshop in an attic with a rusty cocoa tin full of rouge and a jug for pouring [2]. On his account, the old workers polished black stone with red iron-oxide rouge thinned with oil, which sprayed over the shop, their smocks and their faces [2]. Finlay gives the explanation as his reconstruction, not documented history [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Jet is a common dark in our painting archive. In 3,870 of 23,781 museum paintings, about 16 per cent, a color within CIEDE2000 distance 6 of #343434 covers at least 5 per cent of the canvas [10]. It is mostly a shadow color: in 88 per cent of those paintings it sits among the darkest tones of the painting [10]. The 1900s have the highest rate, 22 per cent of 1,674 paintings, 1.35 times the baseline, and the 1930s peak at 24.6 per cent (17 of 69) [10].

Some painters live in it. [[painter:vilhelm-hammersh-i|Hammershøi]] has the color in 31 of his 50 paintings in the archive, 3.8 times the baseline, and his [[painting:smk-KMS1808|Evening in the Drawing Room]] of 1891 is 95 per cent this color [10]. Modigliani has it in 10 of 18, and Pieter van der Werff in 19 of 35 [10]. By country the highest rates are Norway at 31 per cent, the United Kingdom at 28 per cent and Denmark at 27 per cent, though the Danish and Norwegian numbers partly reflect which museums supplied the photographs [10]. It most often appears beside [[gunmetal]], [[charcoal]] and [[denim]] [10].

All figures are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so a match is not a pigment test [10]. To see the color, look in a Hammershøi interior at the doors and dark coats: they sit close to this swatch [10].
